title: Africa’s green industrial future: AfCFTA as passive trade or active transformer?
body:
Africa's green industrial future faces a unique challenge: abundant potential but fragmented markets. Without scale, firms hesitate to invest, skills remain underdeveloped, and industrial capabilities stall.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is often presented as the magic wand that addresses this challenge. By creating continental markets, it can give firms the confidence to invest, enable learning at scale, and allow skills to take root beyond national borders.

But here’s the reality check: AfCFTA doesn’t automatically create demand.

Under AfCFTA, demand emerges only when African states act deliberately and collectively:

- Coordinated public procurement across borders—turning fragmented national orders into continent-scale markets that firms can plan around.
- Regional anchor buyers—from fertilizer producers to steel and cement plants, agro-processing hubs, and transport systems—committing to long-term offtake that justifies investments in skills, machinery, and R&D.
- Harmonized regulations and standards—from grid codes to certification rules and industrial regulations—so firms can produce once and sell across the continent, rather than redesigning for every border.

Without these actions, AfCFTA risks doing only what Africa already does too well: facilitating trade in what is already produced elsewhere. In that scenario, AfCFTA becomes a trade facilitation agreement, not an industrial one.

The strategic choice is thus clear:

- Passive AfCFTA: Scale fragmentation and competition among African producers. Imports flow easily, skills stagnate, industrial capabilities remain weak.
- Active AfCFTA: Aggregate African demand to build African industries, develop skills, strengthen R&D, and create resilient, homegrown supply chains.

Amid fragmented markets that plague the continent, how African states use AfCFTA will shape how green industrialization emerges on the continent: thriving industries or just smoother pathways for imports.

**Bottom line:** AfCFTA can either be a passive trade framework or an active industrial instrument. The choice will shape Africa’s green industrialization for decades to come.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Woubet Kassa, PhD Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Rex Asiama (PhD)
